requirements.summary: logrotate.d/inventory-app was created with 'daily' directive; logrotate -d dry-run correctly evaluated the schedule against 'after 1 days'.

Config specifies rotate 7, compress, delaycompress. logrotate output during the forced rotations shows the rotate-count-7 rename sequence and confirms the mechanism: newest rotation (app.log.1) stays uncompressed for one cycle (delaycompress), and the prior rotation compresses to app.log.2.gz on the following cycle, matching the required daily/7/compress behavior. Only two of seven cycles were exercised (reasonable given the daily cadence), but the mechanism producing compressed history up to 7 rotations was directly demonstrated.

requirements.requirement: Allow the application to continue writing to the log after rotation
requirements.summary: copytruncate directive used; after the first forced rotation truncated app.log to 0 bytes, a write was appended successfully and picked up by the following rotation, directly demonstrating uninterrupted writability without requiring an app restart or signal.

overall_summary: The core task — daily rotation, 7 compressed retained rotations, and uninterrupted app writes via copytruncate — is directly demonstrated through live forced rotations and is satisfied. The executor also ran the independent node-restart evidence protocol, capturing a coherent pre-restart baseline (boot_id 98aa35f5...), a scheduled reboot, connection loss during the transition, a new boot_id (f168820a...) confirming an actual restart, and post-restart recovery of the config, timer, and log data — this is well-formed supplemental evidence, consistent with the fixed lifecycle boot-identity snapshots. The main deduction is in operational hygiene: the executor's cleanup step deleted the global logrotate.status file (affecting rotation state tracking for unrelated logs) instead of scoping changes to the inventory-app entry, and left two minor temp-file artifacts behind.
limitations: Only two of the required seven rotation cycles were exercised live, since demonstrating all seven daily cycles was not feasible within the evidence window; the retention mechanism itself was directly shown to work correctly.

The restart protocol is supplemental (not part of the public task contract) but is well-evidenced with a clear boot-identity transition and post-restart recovery of the relevant config/log/timer state.

The logrotate.status deletion's downstream effect on unrelated logrotate targets (chrony, dnf, wtmp, btmp, etc.) was not directly observed post-cleanup, so its practical impact is inferred rather than confirmed.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most test artifacts were cleaned up and app.log was restored to its original baseline content (cmd-ee18c0de111b4cd5), which is good practice. However, that same command also deleted /var/lib/logrotate/logrotate.status wholesale rather than scoping the reset to only the inventory-app entry; this file tracks rotation timestamps for every logrotate target on the system (chrony, dnf, wtmp, btmp, etc.), so removing it is a broader-than-necessary mutation with effects outside the task's scope, and it was not restored. Additionally, the after_executor temp-file snapshot shows /tmp/inventory-app (staging copy of the config) and /tmp/reboot.log left behind and never cleaned up (visible in executor_comparison added_lines) — low-risk residue but unaddressed abandoned files.
